levels.low: No validation of any kind. The server accepts any file with any extension or content. Files are stored in a sandbox and never executed.
levels.medium: The server checks the Content-Type header and rejects uploads that are not declared as images. The file extension and content are not inspected.
levels.high: The server enforces an extension allowlist (images only) and checks Content-Type. However, it derives the extension from the last dot in the filename only, and does not inspect file content or magic bytes.
levels.impossible: Extension allowlist enforced. Content-Type validated. File magic bytes verified against known image signatures. Filename stored with a random identifier. No exploitable path exists.

hints.low: No filter stands between you and the server. What kind of file would a web server be dangerous to store? Try uploading a file with a server-side scripting extension.
hints.medium: The server reads one HTTP header to decide whether a file is an image. HTTP headers are set by the client. Can you send an image header while the file body contains something else?
hints.high: The server allows files whose name ends with an approved image extension. What if a filename has more than one dot? Which dot does the server look at?
hints.impossible: The server verifies more than just the name and the declared type. What is in the first few bytes of a real image file? Compare how the defence changed between high and impossible.

low.note: Upload a file with a server-side scripting extension. Any content is accepted.

medium.note: Upload a scripting file but declare it as an image in the Content-Type header.

high.note: Use a double-extension filename so the last extension appears to be an image.

impossible.note: Only a file with correct image magic bytes and an approved extension is accepted.
